primers.lede: Fourteen dishes, nine from the Path's first three semesters and five Easy plates from further up, each met when it has been cooked and logged.
paragraphs: At Commis a dish is a single technique with a plate built around it. These are the course's opening semesters and the library's Easy plates: one technique, no wait, put up without notes. Fourteen dishes sit at this level, and most are a pan or a pot you will be handed in your first weeks. What they ask is repetition until your hands stop needing the recipe card.

Take the four from Knife & Fire Foundations first, and take The French Omelette before anything else, knowing it is the one Intermediate plate at this level: eight minutes, and the whole of heat control and seasoning in one pan. Then Ratatouille for the knife cuts and the sauté, Salade Niçoise for blanching and shocking, and Chicken Piccata last of the four, because it is the busiest of the four: a dredge, a hard sear, a deglaze and a reduction on a single pan.

Next come the two soups from Stocks, Soups & the Simmer. Miso Soup teaches dashi and soaking dried goods back to life: fifteen minutes, and the semester's lesson in restraint. Pasta e Fagioli teaches sweating aromatics soft and never browned, the base under most pots in a kitchen. Then the three from The Sauté Station & Pan Sauces: Shrimp Scampi repeats the sear and the deglaze from the piccata and adds the mount, cold butter swirled into the reduced wine off the heat; Chicken Teriyaki adds resting meat and slicing against the grain; and Garides Saganaki brings the flambé and the habit of keeping the cooking liquid. By the third of these, the semester's four moves should be in your hands: sear, deglaze, mount, plate.

The last five sit further up the Path but are Easy plates all the same. Crêpes and Panna Cotta from Pastry Fundamentals are your first precision work: the crêpe is batter and pan control, the panna cotta is a bare simmer held below the boil, a pass through a sieve and the wobble test for the set. The three from The Wok & High Heat, Pad Krapow Moo, Bulgogi and Rau Muong Xao Toi, ask for total mise before the flame goes on, because the cooking is over in minutes. Rau Muong Xao Toi is ten minutes of wok technique, so take it first of the three. Bulgogi is the most layered, with knife cuts, a marinade, rendered fat and a sear, so take it last.

Use the doors in the order they sit. Read the semester opens the Path of Study at the semester that teaches the first dish you have not yet cooked. Cook the next dish opens that recipe. The library at this level shows the recipe grid filtered to this level's difficulty, when you want to choose rather than follow. A dish is met when it has been cooked and logged, and that is the whole rule: a dish you have read is not met, and a dish you cooked but did not log is not met either. Log it the same shift.
primers.next: Chef de Partie holds eighteen dishes, the station's work: Cacio e Pepe, Soupe à l'Oignon, Boeuf Bourguignon and Coq au Vin, Rosemary Focaccia and Crème Brûlée, Jerk Chicken and Cantonese Steamed Fish. They ask for an emulsion, a braise, a bread or a custard held to a standard, on the pan-sauce hands you built here.

primers.lede: The techniques a station runs on all day: the cuts, salted water, the sweat, the sear, the simmer, and the pan you never wash before it has made its sauce.
paragraphs: Take the board first. Knife cuts sit on more recipes than almost anything else here, and the standard is uniformity, not speed: any three pieces should match. Then the pot. Salted water & the float test, blanching & shocking and the bare simmer are one lesson at two heats, the rolling boil and the shiver under it: water seasoned before anything goes in, an ice bath ready before the timer starts, a surface watched rather than set once. Skimming and keeping the cooking liquid come after: lift the foam, hold it below the boil, save the liquid.

The pan is one lesson with three heats. Sweating aromatics is low heat and no color. Sautéing & the shallow fry is a single layer kept moving, light color fast. Searing is the hard crust: a pan that never falls quiet and a piece that releases itself. A recipe that says cook the onions means one of the three; learn which before the rest of the pan. Deglazing & pan sauces, reducing a sauce and making a roux follow: the fond brown and not black, salt at the end because it concentrates, the roux taken to its stage and no further.

Roasting in a hot oven, the broiler and charring over open flame are dry heat from three directions: all around, from above, and straight against the surface. Each has its marks: the oven fully up to heat and air around every piece; the broiler lit first and somebody standing at it, because pale turns bitter in tens of seconds; nothing between flame and surface, no acrid edge. Griddle & plancha work and tortillas on the comal want full contact with dry metal. Resting meat & slicing against the grain closes the roast: off before the target, a dry board when you cut. The fryer is a chain in order: the coat before the fry, deep frying at temperature, draining fried food on a rack, salted within seconds.

Salt, cold, time and hands come next. Salting to draw the water out is salt on every face, somewhere for the water to go, and that water poured off before heat; brining & curing is full commitment, timed against weight and thickness, dried before anything crisps. Chilling to firm and the overnight rest are waiting done properly: cooled fast first, cold through, not cold at the rim. Shaping by hand, whipping a meringue and the wobble & the skewer belong to the bake: matched pieces with sealed seams, stiff peaks with a slight bow, a skewer tested at the true center. Caramelizing onions, brown butter, poaching eggs, trussing, flambé and sourdough starter carry no written standard.

Eight more carry their own marks. Soaking dried goods back to life is tested at the center of the largest piece; steaming is the lid left on over a rolling boil; straining & passing through a sieve and mashing & puréeing are judged on the tongue; dashi is pale gold and clear, kombu out before the first bubbles. Frying the paste until the oil splits, dry-pan toasting and egg wash & the baker's shine each have one signal: clear fat pooling at the edges, fragrance before color, a thin even coat with nothing pooled.

Met has one rule. A technique with a written standard is met when a cook on one of its recipes was graded met against that standard; one without a standard is met by any cook of one of its recipes. Open Read the techniques and work down the index in the order above, the last eight as their recipes come up. Open The next technique between services: the page of the first technique not yet met.

primers.lede: The everyday words: what the ticket says, what the pan is doing and what is on your board, met by recall, never by a miss alone.
paragraphs: Commis holds 266 terms, the largest subsection on this page, and none of them is rare. This is the vocabulary a ticket and a prep list assume you have: the pan verbs, the produce you touch first, the everyday cuts, the tools on the rack and the words for why a plate tastes wrong. Do not read it front to back. Read it in the order the work meets you.

Take Mise en Place first, because everything else assumes it: read fully, prep completely, then light the burner. Knife Cuts: The Classical Ladder comes next, before anything hits a pan: it sizes the dice and the julienne and asks for uniformity before speed. Then the pan verbs. Sweat vs. Sauté vs. Sear sets the three apart by heat and intent, Deglaze & Fond says what the browned layer is for, and Searing & Pan Technique is leaving the protein alone until it releases. Poach, Simmer, Boil are three temperatures pretending to be one method; Blanch & Shock is how a green vegetable prepped at noon plates at eight. Then Roux, Slurry & Liaison for the thickeners, and Roasting, Baking & Carryover, which says pull the roast early and rest it.

Next, the things in your hands. Allium Family and Mirepoix, Trinity, Sofrito & Friends explain why nearly every dish opens with onion in fat, and the Vegetable Atlas, 61 entries and the biggest group here, names each one: Yellow Onion, Garlic, Carrot, Celery, Shallot and Leek. Read Starchy vs. Waxy Potatoes before Russet Potato, and Hearty vs. Tender Herbs before Thyme, Rosemary and Flat-leaf Parsley, because the family entry gives the rule and the single entry gives the reason, and now and then the exception. Learn the fruit, grain and pantry entries the menu uses, then fill in the rest between services.

The cuts run to 25 entries, the steer, the pig, the lamb, the bird and the fish case; start with Chuck, Brisket (Point vs. Flat), Ribeye / Prime Rib, Pork Belly, Ham & Hock, Lamb Primals and Chicken Anatomy for Cooks. The level asks for the reason behind each: Chuck wins at braising because its collagen melts into gelatin low, slow and wet, and it fights you fast. The tool rack is here too: The Chef's Knife (Western Profile), Sharpening: Whetstones, Burrs & the Truth About Honing (the rod realigns an edge, it does not sharpen one), Thermometers & the Instrument Cluster, Scales & Measuring by Weight and Cast Iron.

Finish with the three entries that turn cooking into judgment: Tasting & Seasoning Like a Chef, Salt & Perception and The Repair Table: Balancing a Dish. Flat and salty, the two faults under The Palate on this page, open the Repair Table, which gives each its levers in order of gentleness; the Palate primer walks those levers, so read the entry here for the whole chart and take the two faults there. Read the terms opens the Lexicon at this level; read one group, then go straight to Flashcards and Quiz, both over this level's terms. A term is met when you have recalled it met or close on the flashcard ladder, or in the quiz; a miss alone is never met.

primers.lede: The Floor Deck at Commis is the 110 menu words a guest will ask about tonight, taken by method first, then the cuts, the fish case and the larder.
paragraphs: These are the deck's first 110 cards, one to a menu word. Each card gives a gist, a why and a menu line, and most give the thing it is not. Read the line first, the way the word reaches you on the floor, then the not-this where the card has one: that is what a guest will confuse it with.

Take the twenty methods first; every other card leans on them. Boiled, Simmered and Poached are one ladder of heat in liquid, from a rolling bubble to none at all, and Steamed sits above the water, not in it. Seared, Sautéed, Fried and Grilled are the dry, hot, fast side, with Blackened and Chicken-Fried as two Southern turns in a skillet. Braised is the slow one, half in liquid under a lid; Roasted is the oven's dry heat, fast or slow. Brined, Cured and Pickled happen to food before or instead of cooking; Smoked either flavors it cold or cooks it low and slow. Learn each by the neighbor it is set against: Simmered is not Boiled, Seared is not Caramelized, Cured is not Smoked.

Bacon, Prosciutto, Pastrami, Corned Beef and Chorizo tie straight back to Brined, Cured and Smoked, so take them while those cards are fresh. Then the block: the steakhouse cuts run from Tenderloin, the softest and mildest, through New York Strip to Ribeye, the most marbled, and Porterhouse and T-Bone hold two of them on one bone. Brisket, Short Rib, Shank and Shoulder want hours of low heat, and braised Short Rib has no temperature to ask for. Pork Chop, Rack of Lamb and Duck Breast each say how the kitchen sends them. Salmon, Tuna, Swordfish and Halibut each carry a doneness note, Flounder, Snapper and Trout are the mild, lean fish, and Shrimp, Scallops, Oysters and Clams each carry a sizing or serving note.

The rest is the larder and the dessert menu, fastest by family: Parmesan, Ricotta, Feta and Blue Cheese; Grits, Risotto, Ravioli and Tortellini; Stock, Jus, Hollandaise, Vinaigrette and Pesto; Brioche, Sourdough, Puff Pastry and Tart. Sort the sweets by what holds them: Custard and Crème Brûlée by egg, Mousse by the whipped cream or whites folded in, Ice Cream, Sherbet and Sorbet by how much dairy is churned in. Then Jam against Compote by how far the fruit is cooked, Marmalade by its citrus peel, and Kimchi against a vinegar pickle, the sour grown rather than poured. Among the mushrooms, the pair is Truffle against Truffle Oil.

Save the nine menu words for last: Prix Fixe against Tasting Menu, À la Carte, Market Price, and the claims House-Made, Grass-Fed, Wild-Caught, Organic and Heirloom, each saying one narrow thing, not the wider thing a guest hears. Market Price has a job attached: know tonight's figure before service.

Take the doors in this order. Flip cards is where you read, one section at a time. Say it back is the one deck mode that counts as a round: recall before recognition. The written test is untimed and ends on what you missed with the right answers and no number: use it to find the section you skipped. The deck landing shows what is owed today. A card is met once it has been graded met or close in the deck's modes; a miss on its own is never met.
primers.next: Chef de Partie takes the deck to the station: Confit, Sous Vide, Rendered and Pan-Roasted as methods; Pancetta, Coppa, Pâté, Rillettes and Terrine on the board; Hanger, Skirt, Flank and Flat Iron steaks at the block; Branzino, Skate and Monkfish in the case; and the sauces beside them, Béarnaise, Béchamel, Demi-Glace and Aioli.

primers.lede: Three folios for the first weeks: the chicken on your board, the spices in their whole form and the mushrooms in the walk-in, six subjects to each.
paragraphs: Each plate is a folio: one illustration keyed to six numbered subjects, a guide that names each one and says how to tell it from its neighbor, and a short list of sources for reading further. Commis holds three of them, Chicken: cuts and giblets, Spices: from fruit to flower and Mushrooms: six cultivated market forms. They are read, never graded, and nothing about them is recorded; the six questions at the foot of each folio are a quiet check for you alone.

Take the chicken first, because it is the bird you portion this week. Four subjects are the portions. The breast is the white meat of the chest; the thigh sits above the leg joint and the drumstick below it, both dark meat; and the wing carries the small drumette, which belongs to the wing and not the leg. The last two are the giblets a kitchen keeps. The liver is a soft organ, not a muscle cut, and the gizzard is the thick, muscular stomach that grinds the bird's food, which is how you tell the two apart.

Then the spices, each shown whole before it becomes a powder. Black pepper is the fruit of a tropical vine, and black, white and green peppercorns are one species handled three ways. Cumin is slender and ridged where coriander is round, and coriander is the seed of the plant whose leaves you call cilantro. Cinnamon is rolled bark, turmeric is an underground rhizome, and cloves are dried flower buds with no tie to a clove of garlic. The lesson of this folio is origin: know which part of the plant you are holding.

Leave the mushrooms for last. These are market mushrooms, not a guide for foraging. The white button, the cremini and the portobello are one species in three forms, so the color of the cap is not an age clock. Shiitake has an umbrella cap and a stem that can be tough enough to save for stock. Oyster mushrooms grow in fan-shaped clusters and take their name from their form, and maitake, also called hen of the woods, is a frilled cluster rather than a single cap.

Read the first plate opens the chicken folio, and The wall shows all twenty folios by kind, these three among them. Beneath each guide sits the original poster archive: the earlier poster, its transcription and the correction notes recorded against it, kept for reference. Learn from the six-subject guide, which is the current lesson, and open the archive only when you want the history.
primers.next: Chef de Partie hangs sixteen folios: pork and beef, the Pacific, Atlantic and Gulf Coast fish cases, the vegetables and fruits of five regions, and cheese read through its milk, make and maturation.

primers.lede: Two faults open the repair table at Commis, flat and salty, and each has three levers you pull in order, one at a time.
paragraphs: The palate at Commis asks two things of you. Name flat and salty, the two faults the repair table opens with, each on a plate, and take each of the six tastes on the ladder to rung 1. These two faults come first because a commis meets them every shift: the soup that tastes of nothing and the stock reduced too far that sends the guest to the water glass. Between them they teach the one habit this subsection rests on. Taste, name the fault, pull one lever, taste again.

Flat is the fault where every flavor is present and none of it arrives, the dish tasting like a photograph of itself. Its levers run in a fixed order and the order is the lesson. Salt is always first, because most flat dishes are unsalted dishes. If the plate is already salted, acid is the next lever, not more salt. If it is salted and bright and still flat, umami is the third and the check ends there.

Salty is the fault that reaches for the water glass before the second bite. Its levers are dilute, bulk it out and counter it. Dilute means unsalted liquid or more of the base. Bulk it out means starch or cream, volume the salt has to spread through. Counter it means acid and a touch of sugar, which bend the perception without removing any salt. The potato trick mostly just dilutes, so count it as the dilute lever.

Take flat first. The table opens with it, and its first lever is the same one that causes salty when pulled too hard. Learn to salt in pinches with a taste between each, and you will reach for salty's levers far less often. Then take salty, and read its levers as an order as well: dilute and bulk before you counter.

The two doors do the work. The repair table lists the faults with their levers, in order, so open it with a plate in front of you and walk flat and salty lever by lever until the plate tells you which one it wanted. Calibrate is the tasting ladder, each taste to this level's rung, which at Commis is rung 1 for salt, sweet, acid, bitter, umami and seasoned. Salt, acid and umami are also the three levers of flat, so the ladder and the table teach each other.
Met here has one rule. A fault is met when it has been named on a plate in the repair table, and a taste when its ladder is cleared to this level's rung.
primers.next: Chef de Partie places sour and sweet on the palate, and asks the same of them: each named on a plate in the repair table, symptom first, then its levers in order.

primers.lede: Four things before you touch a station: the danger zone, the two-hour rule, cross-contamination and FIFO, read once and kept for good.
paragraphs: Food Safety at Commis is a short subsection and the one the whole kitchen assumes you already have. Six items sit here and they fold into four ideas: the danger zone, the two-hour rule, cross-contamination and FIFO. The only thing asked of you is that you read it and carry it to the line.

Take the danger zone first, because the rest hangs off it. The guide states it as a band, 4 to 60 C (40 to 140 F), where pathogens multiply, and then states the one rule the band produces: the two-hour rule governs everything left in it. The same clause goes on to the cooling law, with its figures, its shallow pans and its ice baths, but the cooling law is placed at Chef de Partie, so read it now as the shape of what comes next. Notice what the guide states and what it leaves out: the band and the two hours are stated; what a cook does with a pan that has crossed the two hours is not, and this primer does not supply it.

Cross-contamination is the second idea, and the guide gives it three lines and nothing more: raw below ready-to-eat in storage, color-coded boards, and hands and towels as vectors. Read that as two controls and the vectors they answer, not as a full procedure. The guide names color-coded boards without stating which color belongs to which product, and this primer leaves that gap where the guide left it. What you can act on today is the order of the walk-in shelf and the towel on your shoulder: the first puts raw below ready-to-eat, the second the guide names as a vector.

FIFO comes last of the four because it is a habit rather than a fact: first in, first out, and the guide's practical gloss is to label and date everything, with its own aside that masking tape and a Sharpie run more restaurants than any software. The same clause names HACCP as the systematized version, identify hazards, control critical points, document, and names a service-critical and legal-critical protocol beside it. Both are placed at Chef de Partie, so at Commis you take the tape and the pen and leave the system for later. The room's half of that protocol is not deferred, though: Service on this page already asks it of you, in What We Screened and What We Did Not, as the one question you never answer from the app. The clause closes on the line worth keeping: none of this is glamour; all of it is the license to do the glamorous parts.

The doors are plain. Read: the Food Safety page at this level's first slice, and then the whole page, so you have seen where the cooling law and HACCP sit before anyone at the pass mentions them. Met here means you have read it; there is no exercise and nothing is written down about you.

primers.lede: Service at Commis is the words the room runs on, the screen you never answer from, the cut-off you can run and the bottle you can open and pour without ceremony.
paragraphs: Service at Commis is four modules in two pairs. The Room's Vocabulary and What We Screened and What We Did Not are about words: the ones the room runs on and the one question you never answer from the app. Responsible Service and the Law and The Bottle at the Table are about the drink in your hand: when to stop pouring, and the bottle you carry to the table.

Take The Room's Vocabulary first, because it is the first module and the first door opens on it. Its four terms are the pass and expediting, the brigade de cuisine, line slang, and service styles with front-of-house fluency. Its outcome is concrete: you act on "86 the halibut" without asking, you say "behind" without thinking, and you can name who is working the pass. The guide keeps menu format and service school as two separate axes, so state both for your room. Know what it does not teach: "dupe" is glossed in four words, and there is no fire or all-day sequencing anywhere, so reading a ticket is your room's lesson and not the track's.

What We Screened and What We Did Not is one term and one habit: you never answer a guest's question about what is in a dish from the app. The recipe screen is a text screen over the ingredient lines. It cannot see a shared fryer, a dusted board or a supplier's label, and a dish showing nothing means the screen found nothing, never that the dish is clear. The screen names what it checked and what it did not on every recipe, so the outcome is saying that in your own words to the guest who asks.

Responsible Service and the Law is one term from Cocktail & Bar, and its outcome is a cut-off you can run in order: slow the pace, water, food, then a clear kind no with a manager behind you. You check anyone who could plausibly be under 30, you know dram-shop liability makes the room civilly liable for a guest it overserved, and you can offer a good zero-proof or a spritz instead of a fourth negroni.

The Bottle at the Table has three terms: the sommelier's service ritual and floor fluency, wine faults, and decanting, temperature and glassware. The taste pour exists to check for faults and not preference. Corked smells of wet cardboard, oxidized of bruised apple, reduced of struck match, which may blow off if you wait. A corked bottle you replace graciously without arguing. Whites go out chilled, reds cool, just under room temperature. Present, open and pour without ceremony, and that is this module's outcome.

The doors on the level page are The first module, which opens The Room's Vocabulary; The track, all 27 modules; and the Drill, which runs the service drill over this level's modules with the whole track as the field. A module is met through its terms: every term of the module recalled met or close in the drill. The Commis test is untimed, runs across the subsections, and ends on what you missed with the right answers.

primers.lede: Eighteen plates that run a station: the pan sauce, the braise, bread and custard, live fire and the fish case.
paragraphs: Chef de Partie holds eighteen dishes, every one a difficulty 2 plate: more than one technique, a wait or a build that no Commis plate asked of you. They come from eight semesters of the Path of Study, so take them by semester unless your station is putting one of them up tonight.

Take Cacio e Pepe first: twenty minutes, and the test is toasting the pepper in a dry pan, then bringing starch, fat and cheese together without the sauce breaking. Then the soups. Soupe à l'Oignon is ninety minutes of caramelizing onions, a deglaze and the broiler; Barszcz is the same clock spent on the pot and then the sieve, a clear soup that shows every shortcut. Then Sole Meunière, fifteen minutes and the sauté station's exam: dredge, sear for the hard crust, brown the butter, plate.

Four braises sit in the middle of this level. Boeuf Bourguignon, Coq au Vin, Ragù alla Bolognese and Jamaican Oxtail Stew share one idea: browned meat, low heat and time until it gives, and for the beef and the oxtail, until the collagen gives. Take Coq au Vin first, the shortest at 110 minutes and the full sequence of render, deglaze and reduce. Bourguignon runs three and a half hours; the ragù three, and its lesson is keeping the cooking liquid. The oxtail stew is four hours, opens on a caramel, is skimmed as it goes and closes on a reduced sauce.

Rosemary Focaccia and Crème Brûlée stand alone in their semesters and are baking and pastry science at its base. The focaccia is one technique, proofing, stretched over 150 minutes: reading the dough rather than the timer. The brûlée is precision: temper the custard, pass it through a sieve, set it in a water bath, finish under the torch. Neither forgives a rushed hand.

Jerk Chicken, Huli Huli Chicken and Memphis Dry-Rub Ribs are Fire & Smoke: the two chickens marinate, then grill over live coals; the ribs are rubbed dry and smoked low and slow for five hours, so take the chickens first. Then the fish case. Cantonese Steamed Fish and Miso-Glazed Black Cod are thirty minutes each at the stove, once the cod has had its days in the miso, and teach the courage to serve fish barely touched, one under the lid, one under the broiler. Linguine alle Vongole and Whole Grilled Fish with Ladolemono both mount an emulsion, one from clam liquor and pasta water, one from oil and lemon over a fish you fillet off the grill. Calamari Fritti closes the level: coat, deep fry, drain on a rack, never paper.

A dish is met when it has been cooked and logged: not read, not watched, cooked, and the log kept. Read the semester opens the Path of Study at the semester that teaches the first dish you have not yet cooked. Cook the next dish opens that recipe's page. The library at this level is the recipe grid filtered to this level's difficulty. The Chef de Partie test at the foot of the page runs untimed across the subsections and ends on what you missed with the right answers.
primers.next: Sous Chef asks for the long wait and the multi-component build: Birria de Res con Consomé, Pizza Margherita, Country Sourdough Loaf, Baguette de Tradition, Tarte au Citron, Profiteroles and Char Kway Teow, the wok, the wild yeast and the choux this level has not yet touched.

primers.lede: Fifty techniques, and every one of them is what a station is judged on: the sauces, the braise, the dough, the sugar and the spice rack.
paragraphs: Fifty sit here, twenty-one with a written standard; the other twenty-nine are met by cooking any one of their recipes, and the fast way through is by family.

Start with the sauces. Béchamel is the mother sauce on the roux you already own; beurre blanc is reduce, season, mount, plate; hollandaise and building an emulsion are one physics, fat into the water phase slowly under hard shear, and one rescue: a fresh base with the broken sauce whisked into it. Building an emulsion carries the standard, so take it first of the emulsions: no free fat sits ahead of the work, and at the plate it clings and holds a line.

Then the braise. Braising has 39 recipes: deep brown before the liquid, liquid partway up and trembling, never boiling, a fork that twists with almost no resistance while the piece lifts out whole. Confit is the same patience in fat; rendering fat is the step before it, cold pan and slow rise. Marinating carries a standard on 70 recipes and one hard lesson: it works at the surface and no further, and longer is a different result, not a better one. Curing gravlax is salt and time doing the work, ceviche is acid doing it; keep the stated time and the stated cold. Tadka is judged on order and sound, hardest seeds first and delicate last; pounding a curry paste on the smear, hard and dry pounded before the wet goes in.

The bread bench is the biggest family. Kneading dough, resting dough, proofing, scoring, working with masa and pleating dumplings carry standards; fresh pasta and handling phyllo are met by any of their recipes. Take the loaf in its own order: knead to satin and barely tacky; rest until it rolls without springing back, and let fermentation run in that rest as a rate, not a duration: steady warmth chosen on purpose, visible activity, a clean smell; then proof by volume and the poke test, never by the clock. Scoring's standard is written on skin over fat, not on a loaf: one clean draw at a slant on a cold dry surface, parallel lines a finger's width apart, through the skin and stopping in the fat, never the flesh. Masa is corn, not a gluten dough: the pinch that seals, the covered rest, the smell of toasted corn. Dumplings: a dry rim, a closed seam, even pleats.

Pastry carries the last standards. Rubbing fat into flour and pie crust & blind baking share one catechism, cold fat in visible pieces and a cold shell into a hot oven; tempering a custard and the water bath are the egg held gently, a spoon that holds a line and a center that trembles as one piece; sugar stages & caramel go by a thermometer or a tested stage, never by time. Three more are air and a finish: creaming butter & sugar to pale, grown and still faintly gritty; folding stopped the moment the streaks vanish; icing & frosting onto a bake fully cool. The other two dozen, arepas to the tagine, risotto method to ramen broth, carry no standard: cook one recipe and it is met.

Met is the app's one rule: a technique with a written standard is met when a cook of one of its recipes was held met against it; one without a standard is met by any cook of one of its recipes. Read the techniques is the index at this level; The next technique opens the first one not yet met.

Resting dough: the pause that does the work
Proofing: the rise before the oven

primers.next: Sous Chef asks for the techniques whose standard governs a whole service: lamination and letter-folding dough on the bench you built here, tempering chocolate beside the custard you tempered, velveting as the coat beyond the marinade, and then fire and the knife: grilling over live coals, asado fire, low & slow smoking, jerk, wok technique, butchery basics, filleting fish and shucking shellfish.

primers.lede: Chef de Partie is the station's vocabulary: heat and product first, then the case, the bake and the spice rack, each word a sentence you can say at the pass.
paragraphs: Chef de Partie puts 255 terms in front of you, and the count is not the point. Most sit in the atlases: the spice rack, the herb and chile shelf, the vegetable, fruit, fungi, grain and pantry shelves, taken as the menu reaches for them. A smaller core, heat and product, runs every plate on your station, so start there.

Take the heat words first. The Maillard Reaction, Braising & Stewing and Emulsions are the three to explain before service: why a wet surface never browns, why a boiled braise turns grainy, why a sauce breaks. Then Confit and Sous Vide, gentle heat and patience, confit being the ancestral sous vide, and Consommé & Clarification, the raft that filters a stock clear. Velveting & Marinades, Pressure & Slow Cooking, Fermentation & Pickling, Tempering (Eggs & Chocolate) and Infusion round out the set.

The case comes next. On beef, Marbling is the word under all the others: the grading systems are marbling in different costumes, and more of it forgives higher doneness. Flank, Skirt & Hanger obey one law: salt or marinate, high heat to medium-rare at most, a rest, then slice thin against the grain. Dry-Aging is what the guest pays for in the trimmed loss and the funk. On fish, take Fatty vs. Lean Fish first, since matching method to fat solves half of fish cookery, then Round Fish vs. Flat Fish for the fillet count, and Mother Sauce Fish Stock: Fumet, the one stock where speed is the discipline.

Baking science sits at the level's base. Gluten & Hydration is the language the rest are written in: flour choice, fat shortening the strands, water as a share of flour weight. Chemical Leaveners and Proofing, Oven Spring & the Crumb follow, one for the quick batter and one for the loaf, and Caramel Stages & Sugar Work is why the station owns a thermometer.

The atlases are the long tail, and each has a map. For the spice rack, read Toasting, Blooming & the Tadka Doctrine before the single spices and blends, and keep Building the Working Spice Pantry, the atlas's capstone, open as the map: one gives you the sentence to keep, fat carries spices, the other the core dozen. For the Flavor Atlas, start on Tasting Vocabulary & Palate Training, Building Flavor in Layers and Acid Architecture, the three you act on tonight. Across the produce and pantry shelves, Seasonality & Ripeness is the rule the rest illustrate, and menu writing begins at the market calendar. Salt Types & When Each Wins settles arguments: read it with the heat words.

The doors: Read the terms, then Flashcards and Quiz, both over this level's terms. A term is met when it has been recalled met or close on the flashcard ladder, or in the quiz, and a miss alone is never met, so run the ladder and let the quiz catch the rest. When you can give the sentence at the pass without the card, the level has done its job.

cites.name: Infusion: Steeping Flavor into Fat, Cream & Syrup

primers.next: Sous Chef asks for the words that govern a whole service: Lamination, The Wok and Wok Hei & Stir-Fry Discipline, Grilling vs. Barbecue vs. Smoking, the specialist product behind a plate such as Guanciale, Jowl & Lardo or Black Truffle, and the numbers a sous reads in Menu Economics: Food Cost, Yield & Par and Prime Cost.

primers.lede: At Chef de Partie the deck is the menu's second layer: the words a guest points at and expects a sentence back, from confit to 'nduja to pot de crème.
paragraphs: Chef de Partie hands you 122 cards the floor asks about: what the thing is, how the kitchen handles it and what it is not. Most carry a note or a not-this line, and that is where the misses happen: coppa is not prosciutto, ghee is not clarified butter, a macaron is not a macaroon. Wherever a card has a pair, learn the pair.

Take the six methods first, they describe everything else: confit, sous vide, blanched, fermented, rendered and pan-roasted. Confit and rendered pull opposite ways, meat under fat against fat out of meat. Then the sauces, the family the level is named for on its page, the mothers and their children: béchamel is the white base, demi-glace the roasted veal stock reduced by half and the base of bordelaise, béarnaise a child of hollandaise, and emulsion explains why aioli and remoulade hold. The cold, sharp ones travel together, mignonette, chimichurri and salsa verde; coulis is the sweet strained purée under dessert.

Cuts come in two kinds of card: the steaks, hanger steak, skirt steak, flank steak, flat iron steak and ribeye cap, plus wagyu, a breed and not a cut, most giving the doneness the kitchen sends, and the braises, cheek and oxtail, with no temperature to ask for. Meats are the lean, farm-raised ones to explain, guinea hen against pheasant, quail, rabbit, venison, and the plates that need an honest word, foie gras, chicken liver, bone marrow, beef tongue. Charcuterie learns in contrasts: pancetta against bacon, coppa against prosciutto, pâté against terrine against rillettes, soppressata against 'nduja. The fish case is branzino against black sea bass, skate, monkfish, arctic char, blue crab and soft-shell crab, roe against caviar.

Dairy is a ladder of clarified butter, brown butter and ghee, then compound butter, chèvre, burrata, mascarpone and crème fraîche. Starches split into shapes and grains, tagliatelle against pappardelle, cavatelli against orecchiette, agnolotti and gnocchi, then farro, bulgur, polenta and arborio. Mushrooms are foraged, chanterelle, morel, porcini, or farmed, king trumpet, hen of the woods, and the notes on morel and enoki say cooked through. The preparations split the raw plate, carpaccio against tartare, ceviche, tataki and gravlax, from the cooked one: ragout, croquette, roulade, amandine.

Pastry runs from beignets, galette, pavlova and soufflé to the custards, crème anglaise against pastry cream, panna cotta and pot de crème, and the frozen four, gelato, granita, parfait and semifreddo. The pantry is the seasoning rack: miso, fish sauce, harissa, pimentón, sherry vinegar, preserved lemon, finishing salt. Language holds the menu's claims, dry-aged, pasture-raised, heritage breed and day-boat, and the not-this line says what each word is not.

Flip cards first, the whole card, note and not-this included. Say it back is the one deck mode that counts as a round, recall before recognition, so give it the most time. The written test is untimed and ends on what you missed with the right answers and no number, so take it after a run of Say it back. The deck's landing shows what is owed today. A card is met when it has been graded met or close in the deck's modes; a miss alone is never met, so take a missed card through Say it back again.
primers.next: Sous Chef adds the specialist word on these shelves: squab, sweetbreads and poussin; guanciale, lardo, speck, tasso, bresaola and jamón ibérico on the board; bavette and coulotte; turbot, sturgeon, tilefish, wreckfish and cobia; velouté, gastrique and romesco, and the floor card for beurre blanc, the sauce Chef de Partie already mounts; crudo and escabeche; pâte à choux and clafoutis; and garde manger itself.

primers.lede: Sixteen folios for running a station: the two big animals, the three fish cases, the vegetables and fruits of five regions, and the cheese board.
paragraphs: Chef de Partie holds most of the wall. Each folio teaches six subjects with a guide, a line to remember for each and sources to read further; they are read, never graded, and nothing about them is recorded. Read them in four groups, in the order a station meets them: the meat, the fish, the produce and the cheese.

Start with Pork: six useful distinctions and Beef: where the cut begins, because a station orders by cut. The pork folio runs from the Boston butt of the shoulder through the loin and the tenderloin to the fresh belly, the spare ribs and the hock. The beef folio places the chuck roast, the ribeye, the strip steak, the tenderloin, the brisket and the hanger steak on the animal, and its lines to remember are the ones a server gets wrong: marbling is fat within the muscle, the strip loin and the tenderloin are neighboring but separate muscles, and the hanger is not the flank.

Then the three fish cases. Pacific: six seafood identities asks you to read body shape and fins before a market nickname: king is another name for Chinook, and the fish sold as black cod is sablefish, not a cod. Atlantic: fish and shellfish sets four finfish beside the sea scallop and the American lobster, and Gulf Coast: reef, open water and shore runs from red snapper and grouper to mahi mahi, yellowfin tuna, white shrimp and blue crab.

The ten produce folios read in pairs by region: Northwest vegetables and Northwest fruits, Southwest vegetables and Southwest fruits, Midwest vegetables and Midwest fruits, Northeast vegetables and Northeast fruits, Southeast vegetables and Southeast fruits. Each teaches the part of the plant you are holding, the shoot, root, bud, pod, leaf or fruit, rather than a season, because availability moves with the grower and the weather. Take your own region first and read the rest as the menu brings them in.

Finish with Cheese: milk, make and maturation, which reads a cheese through its milk, texture and method before its color: the crystals in Parmigiano Reggiano are not mold, and an orange Cheddar is not an older one for its color alone. Read the first plate opens the first folio at this level, and The wall shows all twenty. Each folio keeps the original poster archive beneath its guide, with the correction notes recorded against the poster; the guide is the lesson.

primers.lede: Sour and sweet are the Chef de Partie faults: the two a station's own reductions and pan sauces make when the ratio slips, and each one is a lever against the other.
paragraphs: Commis opened the repair table on flat and salty, the two faults on either side of the salt cellar. Chef de Partie moves to sour and sweet. What they share: unlike flat, neither is fixed by adding what is missing. Both are faults of excess, like salty, and excess does not pour back out of a pot. The work at this level is learning what stands against each, in what order, and what each lever costs.

Take sour first, the order the repair table keeps. Its symptom is exact: the acid arrives first and is still there after everything else has gone. Fat buffers rather than removes, so butter mounted in or a spoon of cream softens the edge without touching the acid itself. Sweetness is the other buffer, held below the threshold of tasting sweet: you are covering a fault, not making a sweet sauce. Baking soda neutralizes chemically, but pinches only, because it eats brightness along with the fault. Time mellows on its own, if you have any. Read that list as a lesson in restraint: two levers hide the fault, one changes the pot at a cost, and the last is time, which a service never has.

Then sweet. The symptom is cloying by the third mouthful, with nothing to cut through it. Acid cuts. Salt reframes: the same sugar reads as seasoning rather than dessert. Bitterness opposes it directly, and the table names the sources: coffee, cocoa, char. Heat, the chile kind, distracts from it. Side by side the pair is a mirror: sweetness is the second lever for sour, acid is the first lever for sweet. A fault is a taste that leads and stays; the fix is a measured dose of its lever, tasted after every addition.

The subsection opens two doors. The repair table holds the faults with their levers, in order: read sour and sweet there lever by lever, then find a real sauce that shows the symptom and name the fault before you reach for anything. Calibrate is the tasting ladder, and at Chef de Partie it asks every taste, salt, sweet, acid, bitter, umami and seasoned, to rung 2. The ladder climbs all six, not only the two faults placed here: it trains the tongue that will catch them.

Met here means two things: a fault is met when it has been named on a plate in the repair table, and a taste when its ladder is cleared to this level's rung. For this subsection that is sour and sweet each named on a plate, and the six tastes brought to rung 2 on Calibrate. Do the repair table first, because you cannot name what you have not read, and take Calibrate in short sittings between services, since the palate tires.
primers.next: Sous Chef asks the same of bitter and rich, the two faults placed there, and takes the tasting ladder to its next rung.

primers.lede: Food safety at Chef de Partie is the cooling law and the way you actually cool, HACCP as a system, and the allergen protocol, which the guide calls critical twice.
paragraphs: Commis gave you the danger zone and the two-hour rule. Chef de Partie asks you to own what happens to the stockpot after service, because a station makes more hot food than one service eats. Four entries sit here in two pairs. The cooling law and the cooling method are one practice, stated as a number and as a technique. HACCP and the fourth entry are two systems a station runs inside. Take the cooling pair first: a thermometer tests you on it tonight.

The cooling law is the guide's own figure: hot food to 21 C (70 F) within 2 hours, then to 4 C (39 F) within 4 more. The guide gives the two windows and nothing more; how your code counts them is the code's to say. How you get there is the cooling method: shallow pans, ice baths, never a stockpot straight into the walk-in. A full pot holds its heat for hours in a cold room and warms everything shelved around it, the slow cooling the two-hour rule at Commis already governs. Ladle the stock into shallow pans, or stand the pot in an ice bath and stir, and the law becomes something a station can meet.

HACCP is the systematized version of what Commis taught as habit: identify hazards, control critical points, document. Those three verbs are the whole of the entry at Chef de Partie. So read HACCP here as a way of seeing your station, the moments where a time or a temperature decides whether the food is right and the log that proves you watched them. The figures come from your code and your chef, not from the guide.

The fourth entry is the shortest and the heaviest: the allergen protocol, which the guide calls service-critical and legal-critical. The guide says so twice, and that is the whole of the Chef de Partie entry. What you can act on at Chef de Partie is knowing where your house keeps its protocol, following it as your house set it, and never improvising one.

Nothing here is met or missed: food safety is read, never graded, and nothing about it is recorded. The level page opens two doors. The first is Read: the Food Safety page at this level's first slice. The second is The whole page. Take the first slice first, these four entries, then read the whole page once for the gaps, what the guide names without stating.

primers.next: Sous Chef asks you to run the kitchen so any moment is inspection-ready: temps logged, FIFO labeled, hand sinks stocked and used, sanitizer buckets titrated. It asks what you do during a visit and after one, and with an illness complaint: take it seriously and kindly, gather specifics, preserve records and product, and remember that the cover-up is always worse than the event.

primers.lede: Service at Chef de Partie is the glass explained: how a wine is described, the two pairing games, the bottles you will pour, and the cheese board's formula.
paragraphs: Commis gave you the room's vocabulary and the bottle at the table. Chef de Partie asks you to say what is in the glass and put it next to a plate on purpose. Eight modules sit here in four groups: the grammar of wine, the cellar you will pour from, everything that is not wine, and the cheese board.

Take How a Wine Is Described first, because every module after it uses its seven terms: acidity, tannin, body, dry and off-dry, oak, terroir, vintage. You have it when you answer "is it dry?" and "is it heavy?" correctly, know that off-dry is not sweet, and can hear which lever a guest means by "something smooth". Then The Two Games and the Switches. Every pairing is congruent, echoing the dish, or contrast, opposing it, and one switch does the work: salt loves acid and bubbles, fat wants cutting acid or matching richness, food acid demands equal wine acid, chile is inflamed by alcohol and tannin, sweet dishes need sweeter wine, bitter stacks with tannin, umami makes tannin harsh. Name the game and the switch in one sentence: that is what you say at the table.

The cellar comes next, whites before reds. The Whites You Will Pour leads with three grapes, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling, three sentences each, with the aromatic whites beside Sauvignon Blanc. Two facts matter most: Riesling is the answer to chile heat, and Chardonnay's oak level must match the butter level. The Reds You Will Pour runs from the Bordeaux blend and Pinot Noir through the Rhône school and the food-wine trinity to the New World crowd-pleasers; its test is steering a table off Cabernet when the plate is chile or delicate fish. Bubbles, Sherry and the Fortified End sells Champagne as the rescue for almost any plate, not a toast, tells Prosecco from Cava from Pét-Nat, sets Fino beside Manzanilla, and matches Port or Madeira to cheese or chocolate.

Everything That Is Not Wine covers the rest of the list. Beer pairs by its two families, sake climbs a polishing ladder and has a right serving temperature, tea and coffee are a service and not an afterthought, and a guest who is not drinking deserves a genuine non-alcoholic pairing. Take it straight after the cellar, while the pairing games are still fresh.

The cheese board closes the level, and its spine is a formula. The Board: Formula and Families asks for 3 to 5 cheeses spanning milk, texture and volume, 30 to 50 g a head, always at room temperature an hour out, and asks you to place any cheese in one of five families: fresh, bloomy, washed, semi-hard to hard, or blue. It also says why halloumi holds its shape under heat and gruyère flows. The Levant, South Asia and the Americas then covers the cheeses outside the classical board: paneer, akkawi and nabulsi, labneh, the Mexican trio and the American four, including why American cheese is engineered the way it is. Serve them without apology or condescension.

Now the doors. Open the first module and work down the list in this order. The track shows all 27 modules and where these eight sit. The drill runs over this level's modules with the whole track as the field, and it is where met is decided: a module is met through its terms, every term of the module recalled met or close in the drill.

cites.name: The Two Games and the Switches
Bubbles, Sherry and the Fortified End
The Levant, South Asia and the Americas

primers.next: Sous Chef takes the same subject wider: The Grape Atlas as deep reference, the cheese boards by country (The Italian Board, The French Board, Alpine and Iberian, Britain, the Low Countries and the Cold Edge), the charcuterie boards from The Italian Salumi to The Spanish Cure, How It Was Cured as reference, and What Is in the Bottle.

primers.lede: Seven Advanced plates from four semesters: the braise's long wait, the ferments, the pastry builds and the wok, each met once it is cooked and logged.
paragraphs: Commis was one technique and no wait, and Chef de Partie added the braise and the sauté station; these seven are longer, bigger or hotter. They come from four semesters, The Braise, Bread & Fermentation, Pastry Fundamentals and The Wok & High Heat, and none goes up in one pass without notes. The rule is the same as at every level: a dish is met when it has been cooked and logged.

Take Birria de Res con Consomé first. The braise is Chef de Partie ground; what is new is the chain: marinating with acid, salt and time, searing the hard crust, braising until the collagen gives, then griddle and plancha work to finish, with the consomé served as its own component. It is 270 minutes, mostly unattended, so start it on a day off. It teaches the habit that carries the rest: several techniques, one standard held across all of them.

The three ferments belong together. Pizza Margherita, Country Sourdough Loaf and Baguette de Tradition all rest on fermentation: flour, water, salt, time. Pizza and the loaf add resting dough, the pause that does the work; pizza and the baguette add proofing, the rise before the oven; the loaf and the baguette add steaming, the moisture in the oven that lets the crust spring before it sets. Take the pizza first, because at 90 minutes it teaches the dough's schedule without costing a day. Then the baguette at 280 minutes, then the loaf at 300, which needs a sourdough starter on its own calendar, so begin feeding one before you book the loaf's day.

The two pastry plates come from the semester of precision. Profiteroles (Pâte à Choux Master) asks one technique, choux pastry, in 90 minutes; take it before the tart, because one technique held to a standard is easier to log honestly than three. Tarte au Citron stacks pie crust and blind baking, the water bath and whipping a meringue into one build of 150 minutes, and every layer has to be right for the plate to be right: that is the multi-component build the standard means.

Char Kway Teow is the outlier: 30 minutes, one technique, the least forgiving cooking in the guide. Wok technique is maximum heat, total mise and small batches, so the clock is short and most of it is mise, with the flame at the very end, one small batch at a time. Take it last, or on any short day when your mise is complete, and do not let the clock fool you into a half-done setup.

The doors do the ordering for you. Read the semester opens the Path of Study at the semester teaching the first dish you have not cooked: follow it and you take the braise, the breads, the pastry, then the wok. Cook the next dish opens that recipe page. The library at this level shows the grid filtered to this difficulty. Log each dish the day you cook it.
primers.next: Chef asks for the capstone semester and the project dishes of the Advanced library: Tacos al Pastor (Home Trompo), Central Texas Smoked Brisket, Sauce Espagnole & Demi-Glace, Dry-Brined Roast Turkey with Real Gravy, Salt-Baked Whole Fish and Baked Alaska.

primers.lede: Twelve techniques a whole service rides on: the fires, the wok, the butchery knives, the shellfish and the laminated dough.
paragraphs: Sous Chef places twelve techniques a whole service rides on: a grill lit wrong ruins every plate off it. Three of them, Grilling over live coals, Low & slow smoking and Wok technique, carry a written standard with marks you can read before you cook. The other nine have none.

Take the fire first, and Grilling over live coals before the rest, since it carries the most recipes here. Its marks: the fire ready before the food, coals in gray ash with a hot zone and a cooler one on the grate; the grate hot and clean so the food releases when turned; marks browned, not burnt; the inside on target with a thin gradient, not driven through by a flare-up. Low & slow smoking is a different fire: indirect, low and fed with wood smoke, for collagen cuts on a clock of hours. Its marks: thin blue smoke, never white and rolling; a chamber held in a narrow band by the air intake, not by armfuls of fuel; the stall waited out or wrapped through on purpose; doneness read by probe and feel, never by the hour. Asado fire and Jerk sit under the same lexicon entry; take them once both fire standards are in your hands, since asado runs on embers and jerk on pimento smoke.

Wok technique's standard is won in the mise and read in the pan: everything in dry and in order, the wok loud from first moment to last, every piece coated and glossy with no sauce pooling under it, vegetables keeping their color and a bite at the center. A wok that falls quiet has been overloaded and is boiling in its own liquid. Velveting belongs beside it: the egg white and cornstarch coat with a little soda or wine, rested and passed briefly through oil or water before the wok, that gives stir-fried meat its silk.

Then the knives, which come before the fire: the rack is frenched and the roast tied before it meets heat, and a chef who butchers understands the animal a recipe cannot teach. Butchery basics is frenching, butterflying and tying, plus stripping the silverskin that never renders. Filleting fish is the flexible blade drawn along the spine and the deba that heads and fillets a whole fish; your edge is your yield, so sharpen first. Shucking shellfish rounds out the seafood semester. Pick the recipe that makes you do the cut, not one where the fishmonger did it for you.

Leave the pastry for last, because it has no semester behind it. Lamination and Letter-folding dough are one discipline under two names: dough and butter at matched plasticity, cold but bendable, rest between folds so the gluten relaxes, and counted turns. Tempering chocolate has a single recipe, so that recipe is the way in: melt, cool and reheat on the curve so the cocoa butter sets glossy with a snap instead of dull bloom, the same discipline as the custard you tempered at Chef de Partie.

Open Read the techniques for the index of all twelve, and let The next technique carry you to the first one you have not met. For the three with a standard, met means a cook on one of its recipes was marked met against that standard; for the other nine, any cook of one of their recipes.
primers.next: Chef asks for the techniques nobody drills by accident, taught by no semester and on the fewest recipes: Mole, The soufflé, Paella & socarrat, Biryani & dum, Hand-pulled noodles, Tandoor breads, Sushi rice & rolling and The pretzel bath.

primers.lede: The words a sous owns: the fires and the wok, the fold, the numbers on the morning sheet, and the products a station cook has heard of but never had to explain.
paragraphs: Thirty-three terms sit here and they are not one kind of word. Chef de Partie asked you to explain the menu. Sous Chef asks what runs the service: why the brisket went on at six in the morning, why a fish bought at twelve a kilo is costed at twenty-six on the plate. Read them in four groups.

Take the fires and the fold first: Grilling vs. Barbecue vs. Smoking, Wok Hei & Stir-Fry Discipline with The Wok beside it as the equipment half, then Lamination. Each entry gives the discipline in a line: the two-zone grate and thin blue smoke; dry ingredients, small batches and food left to sit between tosses; dough and butter at matched plasticity, rested between counted folds. When a cook asks why the stir-fry steams instead of charring, have the answer without looking.

The numbers next. Menu Economics comes first: food cost, yield and par, the numbers a sous reads; learn yield first, because costing raw invoice prices is the classic mistake. Behind it stand the finance terms: Prime Cost, COGS and labor summed weekly into the one figure operators live by; KPIs & the Daily Dashboard, one page every morning; COGS Control, where actual against theoretical is the leak meter; Labor: Scheduling & the Model, hourly scheduled to forecast, not habit; Vendors, Purchasing & Negotiation, a second source for the critical categories; Hiring, Training & Retention Economics, where retention is a profit center; Kitchen Design & Flow, designed backward from the menu; FF&E, Smallwares & Opening Inventory, the small checks before cooking; and Health Inspections & Crisis Management, where the daily disciplines are the standard the inspection merely photographs.

The third group is product, the specialist item behind a fine-dining plate. Guanciale, Jowl & Lardo is the cured face and the cured fat; keep its line that fat is a cut of meat. Alpage explains why the Comté buyer asks the season of the wheel. Black Truffle and Black Trumpet both take heat: the truffle's aroma is fat soluble, so it moves into butter, cream and egg; the trumpet is bought on condition and never served raw. Three spices are here because they are chemistry before seasoning: Asafoetida (Hing), bloomed for seconds in fat so the funk turns to onion depth; Panch Phoron, five whole seeds whose crackle is the timer; and The Three Heats, so you prescribe linger, hum or flash on purpose.

The rest is the atlas, the entries a kitchen handles rarely: the fruit, Buddha's Hand, Durian, Longan, Mulberry and Seville Orange; the herbs and chiles, Cascabel, Lovage and Vietnamese Coriander; the vegetables, Nettles, Salsify, Treviso and Winter Melon. Each carries one handling rule worth keeping: zest the Buddha's Hand and never look for juice, count lovage in leaves, glove the nettles and blanch them on arrival. Take these last.

Two doors open on the level page. Read the terms first, all thirty-three. Then Flashcards and Quiz, both over this level's terms. A term is met when it has been recalled met or close on the flashcard ladder, or in the quiz; a miss alone is never met.

primers.lede: Thirty-five cards a sous explains in one sentence at the pass: the cured board, the specialist cut and fish, the classical sauces and the plates with a long build.
paragraphs: Chef de Partie asked for the station's vocabulary. Sous Chef asks for what a guest orders once a year and expects the room to explain without hesitation. Read each card's why line as the sentence you will say, and its not-this line as the server's likely mistake.

Take the meats first; a server asks about them mid-service. Squab, Sweetbreads and Poussin share one fact: youth or a gland with almost no muscle, so there is no chew and the final cooking is quick, though Sweetbreads earn a long prep first, soaked, blanched, peeled and pressed. Squab goes out rosy and turns livery cooked through. The cured board is six answers to which animal, where on it, and whether smoke touched it. Guanciale is jowl, rendered and not sliced for a board. Lardo is back fat, not lard, shaved thin onto something warm. Speck is leg cured with juniper and cold smoked, so not prosciutto. Tasso is shoulder in a cayenne crust, hot smoked. Bresaola is lean beef round, cured and dried, not carpaccio. Jamón Ibérico is the black pig's leg hung 2 to 4 years; its white specks are aging crystals, not a flaw.

The two cuts and the five fish are here because most have a nearby cousin the guest will name instead. Bavette is the sirloin flap, looser and more marbled than flank. Coulotte is the cap on the top sirloin, Brazil's picanha, not the ribeye cap. Turbot is a firm flatfish rich in gelatin at the bone, not halibut. Tilefish eats crab and tastes sweet like lobster. Wreckfish eats like grouper but is its own deep-water family, a Carolina catch. Cobia is fattier than most white fish, firm and buttery, and often goes out raw as crudo. Sturgeon has almost no flake, eats dense and meaty like veal, and takes smoke.

The sauces and preparations pair up on purpose. Gastrique and Agrodolce are both sugar and vinegar, one a smooth French syrup, the other chunky and Italian. Beurre Blanc and Meunière are both butter with acid, one cold butter whisked into a shallot reduction and held just warm because heat splits it and cold sets it, the other butter browned to hazelnut over floured fish. Velouté is the mother sauce built on stock, not milk. Romesco is Catalan: dried peppers, nuts and fried bread. Crudo and Escabeche split on whether the fish was ever cooked. Cassoulet is the long build, baked for hours. Bouillabaisse is the multi-part one: several fish boiled hard so the oil emulsifies, rouille and toast beside it. En Papillote is parchment, cut open and not eaten.

The larder comes last: Carnaroli over arborio because it holds its shape, Black Trumpet split and rinsed for grit, Fromage Blanc smooth and set without heat, a Bloomy Rind whose chalky center means young, not faulty, Pâte à Choux with no yeast and no layers, Clafoutis with its cherry pits possibly left in, Mostarda for the cheese board, and Garde Manger, the cold station whose crudo, tartare and oysters go out raw, and you say so. Take them in that order.

Start at the deck landing, which shows what is owed today, and work the Flip cards for this level until every why line reads as your own. Then take Say it back, recall before recognition, the one deck mode that counts as a round, and finish with the written test, untimed, ending on what you missed with the right answers and no number. A card is met when it has been graded met or close in the deck's modes; a miss alone is never met, so a card you fumble simply comes back owed.

primers.lede: One folio at Sous Chef: the charcuterie board by cut and by process, six products a sous must explain without notes.
paragraphs: Sous Chef holds a single folio, Charcuterie: cut and process. Like every folio it teaches six subjects with a guide and sources, and it is read, never graded; nothing about it is recorded. It sits here because a board is judged by the difference between its products, and a sous is the one asked to explain that difference to a guest and to a new cook.

Read it by cut first. Prosciutto di Parma is a dry-cured whole-muscle ham from the rear leg of the pig. Pancetta is cured belly and guanciale is cured cheek or jowl, so the two are different cuts even when both are used for their fat. Bresaola della Valtellina is the beef on the board, a cured whole muscle from the hindquarter, and it is the reminder that not everything on a board is pork.

Then read it by process. Salame Milano is a cured sausage whose fat sits in fine flecks the size of rice grains; Mortadella Bologna is a cooked, finely ground pork sausage set with larger white cubes of fat. That pair carries the folio's main point: charcuterie takes in cooked products as well as dry-cured ones. The guide is a map of product identities, not a curing method, and the specification of the product you serve belongs to its producer, so ask the kitchen which ones the house buys.

Read the first plate opens this folio, and The wall shows all twenty, the folios read at Commis and Chef de Partie among them; read those again when the menu calls for them. Beneath the guide sits the original poster archive with its recorded correction notes, kept for reference, while the six-subject guide is the lesson.
primers.next: Chef holds no folio of its own. At that level the wall is read again with the menu in hand, and the folios become the way you teach the brigade the distinctions learned here.

primers.lede: Bitter and rich are the two faults placed here, and neither reads in a moment: one stays after the swallow, the other only shows by the sixth bite.
paragraphs: The repair table opened at Commis on flat and salty, and Chef de Partie added sour and sweet. Those four faults are read in the moment of tasting. The two placed here ask for more time. Bitter is a hard edge at the back of the palate that stays after swallowing, so you judge it after the spoon is down, not only during. Rich is delicious for two bites and fatiguing by the sixth, so a single taste says the plate is good. That is why these two sit at the sous chef's level: the sous is the one who tastes a portion through, not a spoon.

Take Bitter first, because it has four levers and asks you to choose between them. Salt comes first: it suppresses bitterness outright, real chemistry and not folklore. Sweetness buffers it. Fat rounds it off. Acid brightens past it rather than removing it. Three of the four soften the edge itself; only acid leaves it in place and brightens past it. So when a charred dish or a bitter green comes up hard, salt before you reach for honey, butter or lemon, and taste again after each move. One lever at a time, or you cannot tell which one worked.

Rich is the simpler fault with the stricter answer. The lever is acid, always acid, and there is no second answer to this one. After the acid, and not instead of it, comes something crunchy-fresh. A crunchy garnish on its own gives the guest one bite of contrast and then the fatigue returns; the acid is what resets the palate so the sixth bite tastes like the first. When a braise, a cream sauce or a fatty cut comes up heavy, adjust with acid, taste past the second bite, and only then add the crunch.

The two faults teach each other. Salt, whose excess you named as salty at Commis, is now the first lever for bitter. Acid, which you named as sour at Chef de Partie, is now the only answer to rich. The chemistry is not new at this level; reading a plate over time instead of in a moment is. Spend your first sessions on plates that hold up on one taste and fail on six, or that leave an edge after the swallow, and say which fault it is before you pick the lever.

Two doors open from this subsection. The repair table holds the faults with their levers, in order, and a fault is met when you have named it on a plate there. Calibrate holds the tasting ladder, which at this level asks each of the six tastes, salt, sweet, acid, bitter, umami and seasoned, to rung 3, and a taste is met when its ladder is cleared to this rung. Bitter is on both doors, as a fault to repair and as a taste to calibrate; rich is a fault only, and the ladder does not carry it.
primers.next: Chef takes the palate to spicy and muddy, the faults with the least obvious levers. The slow reading you built here, to the sixth bite and not the first, is what you carry up.

primers.lede: At Sous Chef the inspector is not an event to prepare for: the kitchen you run every day is the one that gets photographed.
paragraphs: Commis gave you the danger zone and FIFO, Chef de Partie the cooling law and HACCP as a system. Sous Chef moves the subject from your station to the whole room, because a sous is the one standing there when the inspector walks in and the one who writes up what happens after. Ten items are placed here: nine are the Inspections clause, The principle beneath it and seven facts drawn from them, and one is a gap. Read the Inspections clause first and in full, because every fact at this level is a line lifted out of it.

The first group is the standard itself. The guide says to run the kitchen so ANY moment is inspection-ready, and its capitals are the point: there is no prep week. The daily standard it names is temps logged, FIFO labeled, hand sinks stocked and USED, sanitizer buckets titrated, and USED carries as much weight as ANY, since a stocked sink nobody touches is a finding waiting to be written. Take this group before the other two, because it is the part you can walk the line and check tonight.

The second group is the visit. During it, accompany professionally, correct on the spot what can be, never argue, get every finding in writing. After it, fix, document, retrain at pre-shift, and treat repeat findings as management failures, not staff ones. That last phrase is the sous chef's line in the whole subsection: a finding that comes back is yours, not the commis's. Read these two facts together and in that order, because the second only works if the first left you with paper.

The third group is one of the crisis playbooks, written before it is needed. On a foodborne-illness complaint, take it seriously and kindly, gather specifics, preserve records and product. Then call the insurer and, if credible, the health department yourself, because the cover-up is always worse than the event. The principle beneath the Inspections clause says why: crises are inevitable, scandals are optional, and the difference is preparation, documentation, and guests first, reputation second, ego never. Read the principle twice.

One gap is placed here on purpose. Sanitizer buckets titrated is a discipline the guide names, but to what concentration it never says. The app does not fill that in, and neither does this page. Knowing which lines the guide states and which it only names is itself a Sous Chef skill, and the level above makes a subject of it.

There are two doors. Read opens the Food Safety page at this level's first slice, and The whole page opens all of it, worth doing once here so the playbook sits on the Commis and Chef de Partie material. Met is simple: food safety is read, never graded, and nothing about it is recorded.

primers.lede: Service at Sous Chef is the board and the list: the grapes behind the glass, the cheeses and cured meats by country, and what is in the well and call bottles behind the bar.
paragraphs: Chef de Partie gave you how a wine is described and the board's formula. Sous Chef asks you to sell off the list and the board from depth. Twelve modules sit here in four groups: one grape atlas, four cheese boards, six charcuterie modules and one bar shelf. Take them in that order unless you work the bar, where the bottle comes second.

Take The Grape Atlas (Deep Reference) first, because the floor uses it every night. Seventeen varietals, Riesling to Zinfandel, and for each you can say where it comes from, what it smells like and what it does at the table. Work the grapes in pairs, Chardonnay against Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir against Gamay, so each has a neighbor.

The cheese boards come next, in the order the page lists them. The Italian Board and The French Board come first and carry the most cheeses: why the crunch in aged Parmigiano is a feature, Gorgonzola dolce against piccante, why Époisses smells worse than it tastes, and how to stop a guest cutting the nose off a wedge of Comté. Alpine and Iberian sells the melting cheeses on their physics and places Cabrales as the blue that outguns Roquefort. Britain, the Low Countries and the Cold Edge closes the boards with Stilton, aged Gouda, and the four that behave unlike any of them: feta, halloumi, brunost, sulguni.

Charcuterie is the largest group and it has an order. Start with The Charcuterie Board, the two churches of whole muscle and fermented salami on one slicer, because its outcome is the standard you hold the pass to: 3 to 5 meats spanning silk, salame, spreadable and a wildcard, 60 to 90 g a head, whole-muscle sliced translucent and salame in 2 to 3 mm coins on a slight bias, everything at room temperature 20 to 30 minutes out and cut as close to service as possible.

After that the modules go by region. The Italian Salumi tells Parma from San Daniele and coppa from culatello. The Spanish Cure gives you the bellota grades and separates Spanish chorizo from Mexican before a guest orders the wrong one. The French Charcuterie is pâté and terrine cut with a hot wet knife, boudin noir explained to a hesitant table, and the foie gras order handled without improvising. Central Europe, America and the Wider Cure places Black Forest ham, the kielbasa family and country ham's salt. Read How It Was Cured (Reference) last: it answers the nitrite question without a myth, and tells you when to hand it to the chef.

What Is in the Bottle stands apart from the boards: for any well or call order, what the spirit is made from, roughly what it tastes like and what it substitutes for. The level page opens three doors: the first module, the track of all 27 modules, and Drill, over this level's modules with the whole track as the field. A module is met through its terms: every term recalled met or close in the drill. So take one module, then the drill, and move on when none of its terms is missed. The Sous Chef test at the foot of the page is untimed and ends on what you missed with the right answers.

primers.lede: Six project dishes, two from the fire and four from the capstone, that cook for a room rather than a plate and run from one hour to a twelve-hour day.
paragraphs: Chef holds six dishes and none of them is a plate you put up between tickets. Two come from Fire & Smoke: Tacos al Pastor (Home Trompo) and Central Texas Smoked Brisket, the semester where live fire is the ingredient and the cook is counted in hours. Four come from The Restaurateur's Capstone, the final semester that cooks for a room, not a plate: Sauce Espagnole & Demi-Glace, Dry-Brined Roast Turkey with Real Gravy, Salt-Baked Whole Fish and Baked Alaska. What they share is not one technique but a plan: five of the six ask you to schedule the day and hold a standard over a long wait, and two are finished in front of people.

Take Salt-Baked Whole Fish first. It is the shortest of the six at an hour and the only one at difficulty 2, and it teaches you to trust a method you cannot see into: the fish steams inside its crust and you judge it by time for its weight, or by a probe pushed through the crust, not by looking. Next take Sauce Espagnole & Demi-Glace, because it is the base a brown-sauce station stands on: a roux, seared bones, then hours of skimming and reducing until the sauce coats a spoon. It is the mother sauce Chef de Partie named and this level makes at scale.

Then the holiday bird and the theater dessert. Dry-Brined Roast Turkey with Real Gravy is the bird: the salt goes on a day or more ahead, it roasts in a hot oven, and the gravy is built from the drippings and passed through a sieve so it arrives clean. Baked Alaska is a dessert made to be seen: a meringue whipped stiff enough to insulate the ice cream and cake beneath it, then browned fast. Both are cooked for a table that is watching.

Leave the two fire dishes for days you own from morning to night. Tacos al Pastor (Home Trompo) is four hours: the marinade of acid, salt and time does its work before the stack goes near the heat, then the stack roasts in a hot oven and the slices are seared hard on the plancha as you carve. Central Texas Smoked Brisket is twelve. Low and slow smoking carries the dish, with a wrapped braise through the middle hours, and the last two steps, resting the meat and slicing against the grain, are where most briskets are lost. Cook the pastor before the brisket: it roasts in the oven and finishes on the plancha, a plate you can put up in one day before you give twelve hours to the smoker.

The doors pick the next dish for you. Read the semester opens the Path of Study at the semester teaching the first dish you have not cooked, so start there and read the whole semester before you shop. Cook the next dish takes you straight to that recipe page. The library at this level shows the grid filtered to this difficulty when you want your own order. A dish is met when it has been cooked and logged: cooked once, honestly, and written down. Nothing else is asked of it.
